answers.answer: No. SCOPe places these three groups in one fold but in three separate superfamilies. The shared four-helical heme-binding architecture is a fold-level (structural) similarity. It is not evidence of common ancestry. In SCOPe 2.08 the fold is f.21 'Heme-binding four-helical bundle' (sunid 81344), in class f (membrane and cell-surface proteins). It has exactly three child superfamilies: f.21.1 'Transmembrane di-heme cytochromes' (sunid 81342), f.21.2 'Fumarate reductase respiratory complex transmembrane subunits' (sunid 81343), and f.21.3 'Respiratory nitrate reductase 1 gamma chain' (sunid 103501). Superfamily is the level where SCOPe asserts probable common evolutionary origin, based on structural and functional evidence. Fold groups proteins that share a major structural arrangement and topology, and that similarity may come from convergence or physical and chemical constraints. Separate superfamilies under one fold mean SCOPe does not claim a homologous relationship between them. The fold shows only that the architectures look alike. The right wording is 'same fold, different superfamilies'. Within f.21.1 the families are formate dehydrogenase N cytochrome gamma subunit (f.21.1.1), cytochrome b of the bc1 complex (f.21.1.2), and the 'automated matches' bin (f.21.1.0). Homology is therefore supported inside f.21.1 only. It is not supported across f.21.1, f.21.2 and f.21.3. Limits: do not transfer function, heme-ligation or quinone-site assumptions, or use homology-based modeling templates across the three superfamilies. Sequence-based evidence of relatedness would be needed first. Any fold-level template use should be treated as a low-confidence structural analogy. Another SCOPe release could revise these assignments, so cite the release (2.08) and sunids.
